name: Sara Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What is your factory work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the morning shift on a bottle-filling line. We fill, cap and label small bottles for several customers, and I sign off the weight and seal checks. My two-year technical diploma helped me understand the pumps, but experience tells me when a nozzle is drifting before the numbers look bad. I am one of the senior operators and am paid toward the top of this work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What matters at home, and how do you feel about new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Luis manages a bakery, our two children are in school, and we have a mortgage. We have about nine months of expenses saved and several other factories within commuting distance. I prefer the line I know and do not use AI tools; a salesman showing a screen cannot show me whether a bottle leaks. I would need a careful demonstration before changing a safe routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my operators to keep their eyes on the seals even if ordering software gets quicker. A customer returns a leaking bottle, not a late spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two incomes and nine months saved make this fairly comfortable. The line still needs physical checks, and I like knowing who is responsible for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep signing off the fill weights and cap tests. If extra paid shifts come up, I would put part of that new pay into savings after our mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. A slower AI future lets me work at a pace where the checks are understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which check do you refuse to skip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cap torque test. A label can be straight while a bottle is leaking in the box. I make the new operator turn a sample cap by hand before signing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for the order paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The clerk can show me the printed order and I will compare it with the line sheet. I have no wish to put an untested answer between a customer order and a fill run.

say: I would **keep** a person responsible for seals and fill weights.
**Faster** order paperwork does not excuse a leaking bottle.
think: The **current** bottle line still values physical checks.
Our **higher** wages and nine months saved make a slow change manageable.
do: **Keep** testing caps and signing off fill weights on each morning shift.
**Add** new extra-shift wages to savings after household bills.
feel: **Calm** with a familiar line and secure current income.
S0.quote: A label can be straight while a bottle is leaking in the box.
fieldNote: **Sara** is a senior bottle-line lead who trusts torque and weight checks more than a new screen.
The **household** has a mortgage, school costs and nine months of expenses saved on solid current income.
She would **add** earnings from newly paid extra shifts to savings after bills.

steps.text: Keep testing caps and signing off fill weights
Save earnings from newly paid extra shifts after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the plant which office work the software changes first and whether a robot capper is actually on the budget later. I want the operators shown a safe run before anyone changes the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My current seal checks will stay for a while, but a capable capper could eventually let fewer operators cover the same output. Nine months saved helps us wait for facts, yet I do not want to lose my higher wage by accepting a vague transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to observe a guarded capper trial and compare its leak results with our hand tests. I would not run its controls without paid supervised isolation practice. If the factory posts a senior quality role, I would apply only if the wage covers our mortgage, its hours fit school pickup and the duties are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about an eventual shift cut, though I can wait for the equipment results. I would rather learn the robot capper slowly and safely than be first at an uncertain control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a short introductory course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hear what is offered, but a talk is not training. If the factory offers a funded paid practical place with a fitter and guard checks, I would consider it. I would not leave my lead shift for a course leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the quality role is not posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I keep my present job and check actual local bottle-line vacancies. There are several plants nearby, but their wages and shift times need checking against our mortgage and school runs. I do not apply on a rumour.

say: I would **ask** for capper trial results and a written rota before changes.
A **robot** should pass leak tests before the factory reduces staffing.
think: A **later** capper might cut my lead hours despite present skill.
**Nine** months saved gives time but does not justify losing a higher wage.
do: **Request** a guarded capper demonstration and compare leak results.
**Apply** for posted senior quality work only with mortgage-covering wage and school hours.
**Check** posted local bottle-line work if no suitable plant role appears.
feel: **Uneasy** about possible roster cuts, careful about safety.
S1.quote: I would rather learn the robot capper slowly and safely than be first at an uncertain control.
fieldNote: **Sara** requests a trial to observe; she has not learned to operate a robot capper.
**Paid** supervised practice and isolation would be required before she handles controls.
An **actual** quality posting, enough pay and workable school hours govern her application; local bottle work is a separate fallback.

steps.text: Request guarded robot-capper trial and compare leak tests
Apply for posted quality role only with mortgage-covering wage and school hours
Check posted local bottle-line jobs if no plant role and wages and school hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the line that AGI can change orders in 2028, but capable robots filling, capping and cleaning around 2031 threaten the hands-on shifts. I want written staffing terms before the machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a serious loss of bottle-line hours once those robots can handle the whole run. My senior pay and nine months saved buy breathing room, but they cannot replace a wage indefinitely. I would worry about paying the mortgage and both school costs if the plant cuts us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would list the family bills and delay the planned garden extension. I would ask for the factory redeployment terms in writing. If it posts a local inspection or maintenance-assistant job, I would apply only with paid safety instruction, pay near enough to cover our bills and hours that work for school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, not helpless. Our nine months saved gives me time to search nearby factories, but losing my bottle-line lead wage would still hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the diploma qualify you for robot maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know pumps and checks, not how to isolate a moving robot arm. I would require a funded paid course with supervised hands-on safety practice before touching it. The diploma is a start, not a permit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your savings on an outside course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first ask for a real funded place and a posted job. The nine months is for our family and mortgage while work changes. I would not buy an unrecognised certificate on hope.

say: I would **distinguish** 2028 office changes from capable line robots around 2031.
I would **ask** for written staffing and redeployment terms.
think: I **expect** a serious loss of bottle-line hours and senior pay.
**Nine** months saved delays hardship but cannot pay the mortgage forever.
do: **Delay** the planned garden extension and list household bills.
**Apply** for posted local inspection or assistant work only with paid safety training bill-covering pay and school hours.
feel: **Anxious** about real wage loss, with time and local options to act.
S2.quote: Our nine months saved gives me time to search nearby factories, but losing my bottle-line lead wage would still hurt.
fieldNote: **Sara** expects major hands-on risk around 2031, three years after 2028 AGI changes ordering.
Her **sizeable** reserve and plentiful local plants temper the worry without erasing the risk to higher pay.
**Any** job application needs an actual posting, funded safe instruction, sufficient pay and school-compatible hours.

steps.text: Delay planned garden extension and list mortgage and school bills
Request factory redeployment terms in writing
Apply for posted local role only with paid safety training bill-covering pay and school hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives the plant time to prove a safe robot-maintenance course, not just announce one. AGI changes ordering in 2031 and capable hands-on line robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 51 near that robot date. I am good at the filler, but a robot cell has different hazards. We can afford to be selective, though I still need an income that respects years of senior work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would accept a recognised maintenance course only if an actual funded place is offered on paid shifts, with supervised lockout practice and a timetable compatible with school pickup. After qualifying, I would apply for a posted local maintenance role only if the pay and shift cover our mortgage and bills. If no safe paid course opens, I would stay on the filler and apply for posted senior operator work nearby if its pay and hours fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautious and somewhat anxious about the eventual wage change. Five years is useful only if the place and job really exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the fitter to watch me isolate the arm, test that it cannot move and reset the guard. Robot isolation practice has to be on paid time, not a video after a night shift. I need a named instructor and a signed assessment before handling a robot arm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a lower maintenance wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not automatically. Luis and I would compare the actual offer with the mortgage, school costs and my current senior pay. If it falls short, I would look at the other factories rather than buy a title.

say: I would **ask** for a recognised paid course with supervised robot isolation.
The **plant** has five years to offer a real place before 2034 robots.
think: At 51, **filler** expertise does not prove robot safety competence.
A **lower** wage could waste the value of my senior work.
do: **Accept** offered funded paid maintenance training only with lockout practice and school-compatible hours.
**Apply** after qualifying for posted maintenance work only with bill-covering pay and workable shifts.
If **no** safe paid course opens, seek posted senior operator work with suitable pay and hours.
feel: **Cautious** and anxious about eventual wages, selective with a strong reserve.
S3.quote: I need a named instructor and a signed assessment before handling a robot arm.
fieldNote: **Sara** accepts recognised training only when an offered funded paid place includes supervised lockout and school-compatible scheduling.
A **separate** later application requires a posted local maintenance job at sufficient pay and workable hours.
**Without** safe paid training, she keeps her present wage and checks posted senior operator vacancies nearby.

steps.text: Take offered funded paid recognised maintenance course with supervised lockout and school hours
Apply after qualification for posted maintenance job only with bill-covering pay and shifts
Seek posted senior operator work if no safe course and pay and hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift that ten years is enough time for a proper transition if the factory puts wages, safe teaching and jobs on paper. I do not want my best years on the line dismissed by a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 in 2036 and 56 when capable robots reach the line around 2039. Our children will be older, and nine months saved gives us choices. I still need to protect the mortgage and the senior wage I have earned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the filler now. If offered a recognised funded course on paid workable shifts with supervised robot isolation, I would take it and then apply for a posted local maintenance job only at bill-covering pay and suitable hours. If no course comes, I would seek posted senior operator jobs at nearby plants on wages and shifts our family can use. New extra-shift pay would go into savings after normal bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary rather than defeated. A long runway and nearby plants help, provided the terms are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach before retiring from this line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach someone to inspect a wet seal and to stop a drifting filler before a whole run is spoiled. Those skills have value even if a robot moves the bottles. I want the new operator to know why we stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you simply live on savings when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our nine-month savings cushion cannot replace years of bottle-line wages. We have a mortgage and children to support. I would use the time to qualify or find a real job, not pretend the account pays forever.

say: I would **ask** for written paid course and vacancy terms over a long transition.
**Experienced** operators should teach seal and filler checks.
think: At 53 in 2036 I **may** still lead the filler while ordering changes.
At 56 **near** 2039, I need paid work if robots take the line.
do: **Keep** leading the filler while checking an offered funded paid safe course and saving new extra-shift wages after bills.
**Apply** after qualification for posted bill-covering maintenance work with workable hours.
**Without** a course, seek posted senior operator work with suitable pay and shifts.
feel: **Wary** of eventual wage loss, helped by savings and nearby jobs.
S4.quote: Our nine-month savings cushion cannot replace years of bottle-line wages.
fieldNote: **Sara** would take only an offered recognised funded course with paid workable shifts and supervised robot safety.
She **separates** a posted maintenance application from a no-course search for senior operator work at sufficient pay.
She would **add** new extra-shift pay to savings after regular bills, while preserving her existing cushion.

steps.text: Take offered funded paid recognised course with supervised isolation and workable shifts
Apply after qualification for posted local maintenance work only with bill-covering pay and hours
Seek posted senior operator work if no course and pay and shifts fit
Save newly paid extra-shift wages after normal bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could remove bottle-line hours quickly. A paid recognised safety course and a real posted job with enough pay would help us keep the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I have no objection to a machine that passes the same leak test I do. A customer returns a leaking bottle, not a late spreadsheet.

headlineQuote: A customer returns a leaking bottle, not a late spreadsheet.
portrait: **Sara** Kowalski, 43, leads a bottle-filling line with a two-year technical diploma and higher operator pay.
She and **bakery-manager** partner Luis have two school-age children, a mortgage and about nine months of expenses saved.
She **never** uses AI tools, prefers familiar checks and wants proof and supervised practice before using robot controls.
**Plentiful** nearby factories give her options, though a future cut to her senior wage still makes her anxious.
Her **next** job depends on a posted role, paid safe training and pay and hours that fit the family.
biggestWorry: **Capable** robots could cut her bottle-line hours and higher wage around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Offer** recognised funded paid safety training and posted local work with sufficient wages and school-compatible shifts.
